questions.text_english:
(1) The United States and China are currently involved in an extraordinary standoff over allegations of espionage through high-altitude balloons. Last week, the US downed three unidentified 'objects' flying over its airspace and that of Canada. The downed 'objects' have not yet been recovered, so it is not clear whether these were balloons.

(2) But the first incident involved a Chinese balloon that Beijing claimed was meant for research purposes and was accidentally blown off course by wind. The US has also claimed that Chinese balloons entered its airspace on at least four earlier occasions, remaining undetected at that time. China, in turn, has accused the US of sending surveillance balloons over its airspace at least 10 times since last year.

(3) Balloons have been in frequent use for several decades now, though the first use goes back by at least 200 years. They are used mainly for scientific purposes, but increasingly for tourism and joy rides, surveillance, disaster relief and rescue.

(4) The bigger balloons can be as large as a football stadium, go up to 40-50 km from the ground, and carry a few thousand kilograms of payloads. Most of these are built of thin sheets of polyethylene, like the common plastic bags, and are filled mostly with helium gas. Balloons can stay in flight from anywhere between a few hours to a couple of months. Those that are meant to remain in air for long, and go higher up in the atmosphere, are made of more advanced materials for increased sturdiness.

(5) Balloons typically have a basket attached to them, called gondolas, that carry instruments or human beings. In unmanned flights, the gondolas are also attached to a parachute. Once the job of the balloon is done, a device in the gondola is triggered to snap its ties with the balloon as well as create a rupture in the fabric of the balloon. With the help of the parachute, the gondola then glides down to the earth, followed by the ruptured balloon. The possible landing zone is calculated ahead of the flight based on weather conditions.

(6) The most common use of balloons is in scientific research. In a way, balloons equipped with instruments were able to perform the functions of a satellite before the space age dawned. Even in the times of advanced satellites, there are situations in which balloons are considered more suitable. Weather agencies routinely use balloons to make measurements of air temperature, pressure, wind speed, direction and aerosol concentrations.

(7) Because of the high altitudes that today's giant balloons can attain, they are considered useful for astrophysicists and even space agencies. These are relatively clear spaces, much above the heights at which airplanes fly and far below the nearest orbits, about 200 km from earth, where satellites are placed. Very often, they offer better opportunities to observe specific parts of the earth, and are also thousands of times cheaper than satellites.

(8) Moreover, because the balloons are brought down after their job is done, the instruments used are recoverable and resaleable.

(9) NASA has a full-fledged balloon programme that does four-five launches every year. Several universities and research institutions also use balloons for research work.

(10) Balloon-based experiments have resulted in at least two Nobel prizes for Physics in 1936 and 2006.

(11) High altitude balloons are tempting vehicles for espionage operations though their use is not known to be very common. Drones and satellites are used more frequently, and spy planes have been in use since World War I. But here again, balloons have certain advantages. They can hover over an area for a prolonged time. Big balloons can carry a few thousand kilograms of payloads, which means they can be packed with spying instruments.

(12) The biggest advantage is the greater prospect of their remaining undetected. Because of their relatively slow movement, balloons are mostly flagged as birds by defence radars, thus escaping attention. In fact, the US has now said it will recalibrate its radar systems to detect slow-moving objects.

(13) Balloons lack the sophisticated navigation systems of an aircraft, drone or satellite, being largely at the mercy of wind speed and direction. But the balloon that was downed on February 4 seemed to have a solar panel attached to it, which has given rise to the possibility of it powering an onboard propulsion device.

(14) Scientific balloons have been used in India for more than 70 years; the first one having been sent in 1948 by Homi Bhabha for cosmic ray research. The Mumbai-based Tata Institute of Fundamental Research started balloon fabrication work in the 1950s and several balloon flights were launched from Mumbai and Hyderabad. It is regularly used by the space institutions under ISRO and weather institutions like the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology in Pune. Institutions like the Bengaluru-based Indian Institute of Astrophysics and Hyderabad's Osmania University, as well as some private educational institutions, also have balloon programmes. In 1969, the TIFR opened a full-fledged balloon plant in Hyderabad, which remains India's largest such facility today.
questions.instruction_line: Based on your understanding of the passage, answer any twelve out of the fifteen questions given below.
questions.instruction_line_english: Based on your understanding of the passage, answer any twelve out of the fifteen questions given below.

sub_questions.text_english: Balloons have been used primarily for :

options_english.D: keeping an eye on the enemy installations.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) scientific purposes. As stated in paragraph 3, balloons are used mainly for scientific purposes, and only increasingly for other activities like tourism and surveillance. Option B, C, and D represent secondary uses, whereas scientific research remains the primary application.

sub_questions.text_english: The advantage of the balloons is that they :

options_english.C: stay in flight for as long as we wish.
options_english.D: are much cheaper in comparison to satellites.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (D) are much cheaper in comparison to satellites. Paragraph 7 explicitly states that balloons are thousands of times cheaper than satellites. Option A is not mentioned as an advantage; option B is partially true but not their key advantage; and option C is incorrect as balloons stay in flight only for a few hours to a couple of months.

sub_questions.text_english: The basket-like 'gondolas' :

options_english.A: can carry payloads and human beings.
options_english.B: have to be manually ruptured after the job is completed.
options_english.D: have a device which is fixed in the gondola to trigger to snap its ties with the balloon.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (D) have a device which is fixed in the gondola to trigger to snap its ties with the balloon. Paragraph 5 describes that a device in the gondola is triggered to snap its ties with the balloon. Option A is partially true (gondolas carry instruments or human beings) but option D is the most precise and complete answer drawn directly from the passage.

sub_questions.text_english: Even after the dawn of the modern space-age, the importance of the balloons has not _____________ .
sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) been curtailed. Paragraph 6 states that even in the times of advanced satellites, there are situations in which balloons are considered more suitable, meaning their importance has not been curtailed or reduced. Options B, C, and D do not logically complete the sentence in a way supported by the passage.

sub_questions.text_english: As compared to satellites, the balloons are more useful to astrophysicists and space agencies because

options_english.B: they provide better opportunities to observe specific parts of the earth.
options_english.C: they don't need large manufacturing units.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (B) they provide better opportunities to observe specific parts of the earth. Paragraph 7 explicitly states that balloons very often offer better opportunities to observe specific parts of the earth. Option A is incorrect as satellites orbit much higher; options C and D are not mentioned in the passage.

sub_questions.text_english: The balloons are mostly used by institutes and universities for :

options_english.A: comparing the cost of launching balloons as compared to spacecrafts.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (B) research work. Paragraph 9 clearly states that several universities and research institutions also use balloons for research work. Options A, C, and D are not mentioned as purposes for which institutes and universities use balloons.

sub_questions.text_english: A balloon is ruptured __________ .

options_english.B: when there is a snag in the operations
options_english.C: to snap its ties with the gondolas
options_english.D: when it is sighted by the enemy

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (C) to snap its ties with the gondolas. Paragraph 5 explains that once the job of the balloon is done, a device in the gondola is triggered to snap its ties with the balloon as well as create a rupture in the fabric. The rupture is deliberately caused to separate the gondola from the balloon so it can parachute down safely.

sub_questions.text_english: The balloons are a more tempting device for surveillance in comparison to drones and satellites because __________ .

options_english.B: they can hover over the area for a longer time

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (B) they can hover over the area for a longer time. Paragraph 11 states that balloons can hover over an area for a prolonged time, making them a tempting vehicle for espionage. Options A, C, and D, while partially plausible, are not the reason given in the passage for why balloons are preferred for surveillance.

sub_questions.text_english: The balloons escape the radars of the enemy as ___________ .

options_english.A: they are flagged as slow-moving birds

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) they are flagged as slow-moving birds. Paragraph 12 explicitly states that because of their relatively slow movement, balloons are mostly flagged as birds by defence radars, thus escaping attention. Options B, C, and D are not supported by the passage as reasons for evading radar detection.

sub_questions.text_english: In para 12, the word 'recalibrate' has been used to mean :
sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (C) readjust. To recalibrate means to adjust or correct the measurement settings of an instrument. In paragraph 12, the US plans to recalibrate its radar systems, meaning it will readjust them to detect slow-moving objects like balloons. Remodel and reconstruct imply structural changes, while rebuild suggests starting anew, none of which capture the precise meaning.

sub_questions.text_english: Unlike drones and satellites, the balloons :

options_english.B: are at the mercy of wind.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (B) are at the mercy of wind. Paragraph 13 explicitly states that balloons lack the sophisticated navigation systems of an aircraft, drone or satellite, being largely at the mercy of wind speed and direction. This is presented as a limitation unique to balloons compared to drones and satellites.

sub_questions.text_english: In India, balloons are primarily used :
sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (D) by institutions working under ISRO. Paragraph 14 states that balloons are regularly used by the space institutions under ISRO and weather institutions. While weather institutions are also mentioned, the passage places ISRO-affiliated institutions first and more prominently. Defence forces and tourism are not mentioned as primary users in India.

sub_questions.text_english: The scientists in India are ____________ about the future use of balloons.
sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) very enthusiastic. Paragraph 14 describes the extensive and growing balloon programme in India, with multiple institutions actively using and developing balloon technology since 1948, and TIFR establishing the country's largest balloon plant in 1969. This indicates great enthusiasm among Indian scientists about balloon use.

sub_questions.text_english: In para 13 the word 'sophisticated' has been used to mean :
sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (C) complex. In paragraph 13, 'sophisticated' refers to the advanced, intricate navigation systems found in aircraft, drones and satellites. The word 'complex' best captures this meaning of highly developed and intricate. 'Complicated' and 'delicate' carry slightly different connotations, and 'expensive' does not convey the technical precision implied.

sub_questions.text_english: Do you think the writer is _____________ the use of balloons for scientific purposes ?
sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (D) advocating. Throughout the passage, the writer presents detailed information about the scientific, research, and strategic advantages of balloons, highlighting their cost-effectiveness, versatility, and India's investment in balloon technology. This strongly indicates that the writer is advocating for their use for scientific purposes, going beyond merely favouring or researching them.

questions.text_english:
Read the following extract from Wordsworth's poem "Tintern Abbey":

..... That time is past,
And all its aching joys are now no more,
And all its dizzy raptures. Not for this
Faint I, nor mourn nor murmur; other gifts
Have followed; for such loss, I would believe,
Abundant recompense. For I have learned
To look on nature, not as in the hour
Of thoughtless youth; but hearing oftentimes
The still, sad music of humanity,
Nor harsh nor grating, though of ample power
To chasten and subdue. — And I have felt
A presence that disturbs me with the joy
Of elevated thoughts; …
questions.instruction_line: Based on your understanding of the above extract, answer any four out of the five questions given below.
questions.instruction_line_english: Based on your understanding of the above extract, answer any four out of the five questions given below.

sub_questions.text_english: What is the significance of the expression : "That time is past" ?

options_english.A: There is some event in the past in the life of the poet, which is referred to here.
options_english.C: An incident which has left an indelible imprint on the poet's mind
options_english.D: Suggests how time has passed quietly

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) There is some event in the past in the life of the poet, which is referred to here. The expression 'That time is past' refers to Wordsworth's youthful experiences at Tintern Abbey, marked by intense physical joy and rapture. The poet is acknowledging that those spontaneous, carefree days of youth are gone, not as a lament, but as a recognition of maturity and deeper understanding.

sub_questions.text_english: What is suggested by the expression : "Abundant recompense" ?

options_english.A: The poet has been amply compensated.
options_english.B: The loss of time is not big enough not to be regained.
options_english.C: The poet has decided not to look back.
options_english.D: The poet is determined to move ahead despite the loss he has suffered in the past.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) The poet has been amply compensated. Wordsworth uses 'abundant recompense' to suggest that though the youthful joys of thoughtless rapture are lost, he has gained something far more valuable in return — a deeper, philosophical understanding of nature and humanity. The mature mind's perception of 'the still, sad music of humanity' more than compensates for the loss of youthful ecstasy.

sub_questions.text_english: What is meant by 'The still, sad music of humanity' ?

options_english.A: Timeless connection between nature and all of humanity.
options_english.B: We should try to find music even in the worst circumstances.
options_english.C: The suffering of humanity is a curse.
options_english.D: We should look on the bright side of things in life which has been bestowed on us by nature.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) Timeless connection between nature and all of humanity. The phrase 'the still, sad music of humanity' refers to Wordsworth's mature awareness of the universal suffering and sorrow that runs through human life like a quiet, persistent melody. It symbolises the deep, timeless bond between nature and the human condition, where nature becomes the medium through which the poet perceives the collective grief of all humanity.

sub_questions.text_english: What do the 'elevated thoughts' suggest ?

options_english.C: ideas which are different from the ideas of others
options_english.D: thoughts which lift a man to go to Heaven

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (B) high and sublime thoughts. In the extract, Wordsworth describes feeling a presence that disturbs him with the joy of elevated thoughts. These are not ordinary ideas but transcendent, spiritual, and philosophically sublime thoughts inspired by the presence he senses in nature. Options A, C, and D do not capture the spiritual and elevated quality Wordsworth intends.

sub_questions.text_english: The word 'subdue' suggests
sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (D) suppress. In the extract, 'subdue' is used to describe the power of the still, sad music of humanity to chasten and subdue — meaning to calm, tame, or suppress agitation or pride. Options A, B, and C (impel, persuade, goad) all suggest encouraging or driving someone forward, which is the opposite of what 'subdue' conveys.

questions.solution: Extract-based question set from Wordsworth's 'Tintern Abbey'. Answers are provided in sub_questions.

questions.text_english:
(1) The Shimla hills are as beautiful as before, but the city has become crowded and its traffic messy. The local population has crossed 3 lakh, with more than 70,000 registered vehicles, and on top of that about 40 lakh tourists troop in every year.

(2) The rush is beyond the carrying capacity of Shimla's narrow hill roads, and several proposals have been made in the past to decongest them with better public transport. Those proposals looked good on paper, but did not materialise.

(3) The Himachal Pradesh Government has now decided to lift some of Shimla's traffic load off the ground with a network of ropeways.

(4) The ropeway decision follows from the realisation that some of public transport solutions that work well in the plains, such as Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), monorail and metro, are not feasible in the hills due to geographical and geotechnical limitations. Hence the Himachal Pradesh Government has sent a proposal to the New Development Bank (NDB) for bilateral funding of the ropeway project.

(5) The Centre's Department of Economic Affairs recently gave in-principle approval for the ropeway project that would start from Taradevi and have infrastructure like smart parking, lifts and escalators to integrate it with the existing transport networks.

(6) The ropeway fare would also be more or less at par with conventional transportation to encourage local residents to use it rather than their private vehicles. The fare for journeys of up to 10 km would be Rs. 50.

(7) This project will benefit the public in the real sense. Besides saving travel time, it would also be beneficial from the environmental point of view.

(8) The almost 15 km long ropeway is likely to be built in five years, and it will reduce transport emissions in the city. The improved air quality will also have a positive impact on people's health.
questions.instruction_line: Based on your understanding of the passage, answer any four out of the five questions given below.
questions.instruction_line_english: Based on your understanding of the passage, answer any four out of the five questions given below.

sub_questions.text_english: Traffic is messy in Shimla because of :

options_english.D: people who do not follow traffic rules.

sub_questions.solution: The correct answer is (A) the narrow roads. Paragraph 2 states that the rush is beyond the carrying capacity of Shimla's narrow hill roads. While registered vehicles are high in number, the primary cause of traffic congestion is the structural limitation of the narrow hill roads that cannot accommodate the volume of traffic. Options B and D are not mentioned in the passage.

sub_questions.text_english: What action has the Himachal Pradesh Government decided to take to reduce some of Shimla's traffic load ?

key_points: The government has decided to build a network of ropeways.
The ropeway will start from Taradevi and integrate with existing transport.
Funding is being sought from the New Development Bank (NDB).

sub_questions.solution: The Himachal Pradesh Government has decided to build a network of ropeways to lift some of Shimla's traffic load off the ground. Since conventional solutions like BRT, monorail and metro are not feasible in the hilly terrain, the government has sent a proposal to the New Development Bank for bilateral funding of this ropeway project, which will start from Taradevi.

sub_questions.text_english: State True or False. The following question could have been part of the above decision making process. Would it be better to consider an underground tunnel instead of a ropeway ?
sub_questions.solution: True. Paragraph 4 explains that the ropeway decision was made after realising that conventional public transport solutions are not feasible in the hills due to geographical and geotechnical limitations. An underground tunnel, as an alternative to a ropeway, is also a terrain-specific solution and could logically have been considered and debated during the same decision-making process before the ropeway option was finalised.

sub_questions.text_english: Complete the following statement : The ropeway will be popular in Shimla _________ .

fill_values: because its fare will be comparable to conventional transport and it will save travel time while reducing pollution

sub_questions.solution: The ropeway will be popular in Shimla because its fare will be at par with conventional transport (Rs. 50 for up to 10 km), it will save travel time, and it will offer an environmentally friendly alternative to private vehicles, benefiting both commuters and the city's air quality.

sub_questions.text_english: State a point in support of the given opinion. The general public would prefer to travel by ropeway.

key_points: Ropeway fare will be at par with conventional transport (Rs. 50 for up to 10 km).
It will save travel time.
It is environmentally beneficial and will improve air quality.

sub_questions.solution: The general public would prefer to travel by ropeway because the fare has been kept comparable to conventional transportation at Rs. 50 for journeys up to 10 km. Additionally, it will save significant travel time compared to navigating Shimla's congested narrow roads, making it a convenient and affordable option for daily commuters.

questions.text_english: Transform the following sentences according to the instructions given against each one. Attempt any eight out of the ten questions that follow.
questions.instruction_line: Attempt any eight out of the ten questions that follow.
questions.instruction_line_english: Attempt any eight out of the ten questions that follow.

sub_questions.text_english: Ashoka was one of the greatest Indian emperors. (Begin : Ashoka was greater . . .)

fill_values: Ashoka was greater than most other Indian emperors.

sub_questions.solution: Ashoka was greater than most other Indian emperors. The rule applied here is the transformation from superlative degree ('one of the greatest') to comparative degree. 'One of the greatest' implies that many are great, so in comparative form we say 'greater than most other' to retain the same meaning.

sub_questions.text_english: Death before dishonour ! (Begin : I prefer . . .)
sub_questions.solution: I prefer death to dishonour. The exclamatory sentence expressing a value judgment is transformed into a statement of preference. The structure 'prefer X to Y' is used, where 'death' is preferred over 'dishonour'.

sub_questions.text_english: On condition of your signing this receipt, I shall pay you the money. (Begin : I shall . . .)

fill_values: I shall pay you the money if you sign this receipt.

sub_questions.solution: I shall pay you the money if you sign this receipt. The phrase 'on condition of your signing' is a prepositional phrase expressing a condition, which is rewritten using the conditional conjunction 'if' followed by a finite clause 'you sign this receipt'.

sub_questions.text_english: Can this news even be true ? (Begin : This . . .)

fill_values: This news can hardly be true.

sub_questions.solution: This news can hardly be true. The interrogative sentence expressing disbelief is transformed into an assertive sentence. The rhetorical question 'Can this even be true?' implies strong doubt, which is conveyed in the assertive form using the adverb 'hardly' to express near-impossibility.

sub_questions.text_english: He forcibly made his way through the crowd. (Begin : He forced . . . )

fill_values: He forced his way through the crowd.

sub_questions.solution: He forced his way through the crowd. The adverb 'forcibly' modifying 'made' is replaced by the verb 'forced', which already contains the sense of force within it. The idiom 'force one's way' is the standard expression for making progress through a crowd by using pressure or strength.

sub_questions.text_english: Only children will enjoy this movie. (Begin : None . . .)

fill_values: None but children will enjoy this movie.

sub_questions.solution: None but children will enjoy this movie. The word 'only' is replaced by the negative construction 'none but', which conveys the same exclusive meaning. 'None but children' means no one except children, preserving the original sense that only children will enjoy this movie.

sub_questions.text_english: I love her more than you do. (Begin: You . . .)

fill_values: You do not love her as much as I do.

sub_questions.solution: You do not love her as much as I do. The comparative sentence using 'more than' is transformed into a negative sentence using 'not as much as'. The meaning is preserved: the original says I love her more, and the transformed sentence says you do not love her as much as I do.

sub_questions.text_english: He is so simple that he cannot see through the game. (Begin : He is . . .)

fill_values: He is too simple to see through the game.

sub_questions.solution: He is too simple to see through the game. The 'so...that...cannot' construction is transformed into the 'too...to' construction. Both convey the idea that his simplicity prevents him from understanding the trick being played. The transformation uses 'too' before the adjective and 'to' before the infinitive.

sub_questions.text_english: The boy saw his mistake. He grew nervous. (Begin : On seeing . . .)

fill_values: On seeing his mistake, the boy grew nervous.

sub_questions.solution: On seeing his mistake, the boy grew nervous. Two simple sentences are combined into one using the gerund phrase 'on seeing'. The preposition 'on' followed by the gerund 'seeing' expresses the immediate cause and effect relationship between the two actions, replacing the simple sequential structure.

sub_questions.text_english: There was no evidence against him. He was acquitted of the charge. (Begin : There being . . .)

fill_values: There being no evidence against him, he was acquitted of the charge.

sub_questions.solution: There being no evidence against him, he was acquitted of the charge. The two sentences are joined using an absolute phrase beginning with 'There being'. The construction 'there being + noun phrase' functions as an absolute participial phrase that explains the reason for the main clause, replacing the two separate sentences while preserving their causal relationship.

sub_questions.text_english:
"Life is like riding a bicycle. To keep your balance, you must keep moving." (Albert Einstein)

There are occasions in life when, instead of moving ahead, we stop moving. The writer says that in order to achieve our goal, we must keep moving despite setbacks. In order to progress, movement is imperative. The issue is whether it is really possible to move when the pressure of movement becomes unbearable. How should we act to keep a fine balance so that our life does not get upset ?

Plan your response and write an essay to explain your views on the issue. Be sure to specifically support your position with examples and points. (You may use examples from your readings, observations and personal inputs)

key_points: Introduce Einstein's metaphor and its relevance to life.
Acknowledge that setbacks make movement difficult.
Argue that perseverance and resilience are necessary.
Support with examples — personal, historical, or literary.
Conclude that balance is achieved through continuous, mindful effort.

sub_questions.solution:
Albert Einstein's metaphor comparing life to a bicycle ride holds profound wisdom. Just as a cyclist must keep pedalling to maintain balance, we must keep moving forward in life to avoid falling. There are moments when the weight of failure, loss or fatigue makes progress seem impossible. Yet it is precisely at such moments that movement becomes most crucial.

History offers us inspiring examples. Abraham Lincoln faced repeated political defeats before becoming one of America's greatest presidents. Thomas Edison failed thousands of times before inventing the light bulb. These individuals did not stop; they adjusted their speed, changed direction when necessary, but never ceased moving.

Keeping balance does not mean moving recklessly. It means setting realistic goals, accepting setbacks as stepping stones, and maintaining steady effort. When pressure becomes unbearable, we must pause briefly to reassess, not to give up. Life rewards those who keep pedalling, no matter how slowly.

sub_questions.text_english:
"Great things never came from comfort zones." (Anonymous)

We can achieve our goal only by endeavouring constantly without caring for the setbacks. Once we relax in our efforts, we risk the achievement of our mission. The issue is : man is by nature out to live in comfort zones. What is it that inspires us to get out of the comfort zone ? Support your position with reasoning and examples taken from your reading, studies, experience or observations.

key_points: Define the comfort zone and its natural appeal.
Explain why staying in it limits growth and achievement.
Identify what motivates people to step out — ambition, necessity, inspiration.
Provide examples from history, literature, or personal experience.
Conclude that greatness demands the courage to embrace discomfort.

sub_questions.solution:
The comfort zone is that safe, familiar space where we feel secure and unchallenged. While it offers peace, it also imprisons potential. The anonymous quote reminds us that every great achievement in history was born out of someone's willingness to step beyond what felt safe.

Human beings are naturally inclined toward comfort and routine. Yet it is ambition, the desire to make a difference, or sometimes sheer necessity that compels us to break free. Nelson Mandela left a comfortable life to fight apartheid. Marie Curie challenged the male-dominated world of science at enormous personal cost. Both proved that greatness demands sacrifice of comfort.

What inspires us to leave the comfort zone is the recognition that our true potential lies just beyond our fears. Failure and uncertainty are not enemies but companions on the path to excellence. The willingness to face discomfort with courage is ultimately what separates the extraordinary from the ordinary.

sub_questions.text_english:
"A leader is one who knows the way, goes the way, and shows the way." (John C.)

Leadership qualities are not found in everyone. It is a rare quality. And such an individual alone has the vision and clarity about their goals. Such a person alone can guide others for they know what is the right path. The issue is how difficult it is to have a clear vision. What are the efforts that will make a person such an individual ? Support your views and reasoning with examples taken from your readings, observations or personal experiences.

key_points: Define true leadership as knowing, doing, and showing the way.
Explain that clear vision is the foundation of leadership.
Discuss efforts required — self-discipline, empathy, continuous learning.
Support with examples of great leaders.
Conclude that leadership is developed through consistent effort and clarity of purpose.

sub_questions.solution:
John C. Maxwell's definition of a leader captures the essence of true leadership: it requires knowledge, action, and the ability to inspire others. A leader is not merely someone who gives directions; they are someone who walks the path themselves and illuminates it for others.

Vision is the cornerstone of leadership. Without clarity of purpose, even the most energetic person becomes directionless. Leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar possessed an unwavering vision of justice and dignity, which gave them the strength to lead millions through adversity.

Becoming such a leader requires constant self-discipline, the courage to make difficult decisions, empathy to understand others' struggles, and a commitment to lifelong learning. Leadership is not inherited; it is cultivated through experience, reflection, and service. Every individual who develops these qualities can aspire to lead, because leadership is ultimately about character, not position.

sub_questions.text_english:
"Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm." (Winston Churchill)

It is said that failures are the pillars of success. If we get defeated by our failures and are deterred from moving on in life, we will miss the glories of success. Therefore, it is necessary that we don't get disheartened by failures. We can do this if we don't let our enthusiasm relax. It is indeed a great challenge. How to face this challenge, that is the question. Plan and write an essay on which you develop your point of view on this issue. Support your reasoning with examples from your readings, observations or personal experiences.

key_points: Introduce Churchill's quote and its meaning.
Establish that failure is inevitable but not final.
Explain how enthusiasm sustains effort through repeated failure.
Use examples of individuals who succeeded after multiple failures.
Conclude with the message that persistence and enthusiasm are the keys to success.

sub_questions.solution:
Winston Churchill's remarkable observation about success reveals a truth that history repeatedly confirms: the path to achievement is paved with failures met with unbroken enthusiasm. Success is not the absence of failure but the refusal to be extinguished by it.

Failure is inevitable. Every great scientist, artist, and leader has experienced it. J.K. Rowling's first Harry Potter manuscript was rejected by twelve publishers. Walt Disney was once told he lacked creativity. Yet both persisted because their enthusiasm for their work never faltered. It was this inner fire that transformed repeated failure into extraordinary success.

The greatest challenge in failure is the erosion of self-belief. To combat this, one must cultivate resilience — the ability to view each failure as a lesson rather than a verdict. Setting smaller milestones, surrounding oneself with encouraging people, and reminding oneself of past progress all help sustain enthusiasm. As Churchill's own extraordinary life demonstrated, the person who never gives up ultimately wins.

SCHOOL BUS RAMS TRUCK ON HIGHWAY; SEVERAL CHILDREN INJURED
By Rahul Sharma | New Delhi, 15 March 2024

A horrifying collision between a school bus and a speeding truck on the National Highway 48 near Gurgaon on Thursday morning left twelve students injured, three of them critically. The accident occurred at approximately 7:45 a.m. when the truck reportedly jumped a red light and rammed into the school bus carrying forty-two students to their school.

The impact damaged the front portion of the bus severely. Emergency services arrived within twenty minutes. The injured students were rushed to Medanta Hospital, where doctors confirmed three children were in a serious but stable condition. Police have registered a case against the truck driver, who fled the scene and was later apprehended.

Eyewitnesses reported that the truck was moving at an excessive speed. 'It was terrifying,' said one survivor. Authorities have called for stricter enforcement of traffic rules near school zones.

sub_questions.text_english:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:

Usually after breakfast on Sunday, he and his wife took a walk in Central Park, or, when the weather was mild, went to the Palisades. But today Solomon Margolin lingered in bed. During the years, he had stopped attending the functions of the Senciminer Society; meanwhile, the town of Sencimin had been destroyed. His family there had been tortured, burned, gassed. Many Senciminers had survived, and, later, come to America from the camps, but most of them were younger people whom he, Solomon, had not known in the old country. Tonight everyone would be there; the Senciminers belonging to the bride's family, and the Tereshpolers belonging to the groom's. He knew how they would pester him, reproach him for growing aloof, drop hints that he was a snob. They would address him familiarly, slap him on the back, drag him off to dance. Well, even so, he had to go to Sylvia's wedding. He had already sent out the present.

(i) What was the reason for Dr. Margolin to linger in bed after his breakfast ?
(ii) Who destroyed the town of Sencimin and why ?
(iii) Who did Dr. Margolin expect to meet at the wedding ?
(iv) What is the significance of the words 'He had already sent out the present' ?
(v) Who were the Senciminers and why did they settle in New York ?
(vi) Find the word in the extract which is opposite in meaning to the word 'perished'.

key_points: (i) He lingered because he was reluctant to attend the wedding and face people from his past.
(ii) The Nazis destroyed Sencimin during the Holocaust, killing and torturing its Jewish residents.
(iii) He expected to meet Senciminers from the bride's family and Tereshpolers from the groom's family.
(iv) It shows his sense of obligation — he felt compelled to attend but had covered his social duty by sending a gift.
(v) Senciminers were Jewish survivors from the Polish town of Sencimin who fled to America after the Holocaust.
(vi) 'Survived' is the antonym of 'perished'.

sub_questions.solution:
(i) Dr. Margolin lingered in bed because he was deeply reluctant to attend Sylvia's wedding. He had withdrawn from the Senciminer Society over the years and was dreading the social pressure he would face from people who would reproach him for his aloofness.

(ii) The town of Sencimin was destroyed by the Nazis during the Holocaust. The Jewish community there, including Margolin's own family, was subjected to torture, burning and gassing as part of the systematic genocide.

(iii) Dr. Margolin expected to meet Senciminers belonging to the bride's family and Tereshpolers belonging to the groom's family — survivors and their descendants who had emigrated to America.

(iv) The words 'He had already sent out the present' suggest that Margolin felt socially obligated to attend but had already discharged part of his duty. It reveals his ambivalence: attending reluctantly while having already fulfilled a conventional social expectation.

(v) The Senciminers were Jewish residents of the Polish town of Sencimin who survived the Nazi Holocaust. They settled in New York as refugees seeking safety and a new life after the destruction of their homeland and community.

(vi) The word 'survived' is the antonym of 'perished'.

sub_questions.text_english:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:

After lunch, during the inevitable stroll along the Ramblas, I lagged behind with Frau Frieda so that we could renew our memories with no other ears listening. She told me she had sold her properties in Austria and retired to Oporto, in Portugal, where she lived in a house that she described as a fake castle on a hill, from which one could see all the way across the ocean to the Americas. Although she did not say so, her conversation made it clear that, dream by dream, she had taken over the entire fortune of her ineffable patrons in Vienna. That did not surprise me, however, because I had always thought her dreams were no more than a stratagem for surviving. And I told her so.

She laughed her irresistible laugh. 'You're as impudent as ever,' she said. And said no more, because the rest of the group had stopped to wait for Neruda to finish talking in Chilean slang to the parrots along the Rambla de los Pajaros. When we resumed our conversation, Frau Frieda changed the subject.

(i) Explain the 'inevitable stroll'.
(ii) Why did the writer lag behind others in the company of Frau Frieda ?
(iii) How was Frau Frieda able to grab the property of her 'ineffable patrons' ?
(iv) Why did the writer think that Frau Frieda's dream telling was only a clever trick to earn money ?
(v) Why did Frau Frieda change the topic she was discussing with the writer ?
(vi) Which word can be a good synonym for the word 'Stratagem' ? (a) Frankness (b) Stagnation (c) Discord (d) Artifice

key_points: (i) 'Inevitable stroll' means the customary after-lunch walk that the group always took — a predictable, regular occurrence.
(ii) He lagged behind to speak privately with Frau Frieda and reminisce without others overhearing.
(iii) She used her dream-telling to manipulate her wealthy patrons psychologically, gradually acquiring their fortune.
(iv) The writer had always believed her dreams were a calculated survival strategy, not genuine visions.
(v) She changed the subject because the rest of the group rejoined them, ending their private conversation.
(vi) (d) Artifice — a stratagem is a clever trick or cunning plan, synonymous with artifice.

sub_questions.solution:
(i) The 'inevitable stroll' refers to the customary walk along the Ramblas that the group took after every lunch. The word 'inevitable' suggests it was a fixed, predictable ritual that always happened — something the group did without fail.

(ii) The writer lagged behind with Frau Frieda so that they could speak privately and revisit shared memories without anyone else listening to their conversation.

(iii) Frau Frieda used her dream-telling as a psychological tool to influence and manipulate her wealthy patrons in Vienna. By interpreting dreams in ways that served her interests, she gradually gained their trust and, over time, took over their entire fortune.

(iv) The writer had always believed Frau Frieda's dreams were a calculated stratagem — a clever survival mechanism rather than genuine visions. Her current wealth confirmed this suspicion: she had used the pretence of dream interpretation purely as a means to financial security.

(v) Frau Frieda changed the subject because their private conversation was interrupted when the rest of the group stopped to wait for Neruda. Once others were present, the intimate discussion could not continue.

(vi) (d) Artifice. A stratagem is a cunning plan or clever trick, and 'artifice' captures this meaning of calculated deception most accurately.

sub_questions.text_english:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:

Or listen to the clock towers
of any old well-managed city
beating their gongs round the clock, each slightly
off the others' time, deeper or lighter
in its bronze, beating out a different
sequence each half-hour, out of the accidents
of alloy, a maker's shaking hand
in Switzerland, or the mutual distances
commemorating a donor's whim,
the perennial feuds and seasonal alliance
of Hindu, Christian and Muslim —
cut off sometimes by a change of wind,
a change of mind, or a siren
between the pieces of a backstreet quarrel.
One day you look up and see one of them
eyeless, silent, a zigzag sky showing
through the knocked-out clockwork, after a riot,
a peace-march time bomb, or a precise act
Of nature in a night of lightnings.

(i) Do you think the city is really well-managed ?
(ii) What are perennial feuds and seasonal alliances ?
(iii) Why does the poet mention 'Switzerland' ?
(iv) Explain the phrase 'change of wind' with reference to the extract.
(v) What does one look up and see after a riot ?
(vi) Pick out the word from the extract which is an apt synonym of the word 'celebrating'.

key_points: (i) No — the 'well-managed' is ironic; the city is actually riven by communal tensions and violence.
(ii) Perennial feuds are long-standing, unending conflicts; seasonal alliances are temporary and opportunistic partnerships.
(iii) Switzerland is mentioned as the origin of precision clocks, symbolising manufactured order imposed on a disordered world.
(iv) 'Change of wind' refers to a sudden shift in circumstances or political atmosphere that disrupts communal harmony.
(v) After a riot, one sees the clock tower eyeless and silent, its clockwork knocked out, with a zigzag of sky visible through the damage.
(vi) 'Commemorating' is an apt synonym for 'celebrating'.

sub_questions.solution:
(i) No, the city is not really well-managed. The description of the city as 'well-managed' is deeply ironic. Beneath the surface of orderly clock towers lie perennial feuds, communal tensions between Hindus, Christians and Muslims, backstreet quarrels, and the ever-present threat of riots. The city's apparent order masks deep social fragmentation.

(ii) Perennial feuds are long-standing, enduring conflicts that never fully resolve — the chronic religious and communal tensions among different groups. Seasonal alliances, by contrast, are temporary, convenient partnerships formed between these same groups when circumstances demand cooperation, only to dissolve when no longer useful.

(iii) Switzerland is mentioned as the origin of precision clocks — symbols of manufactured order, accuracy, and human control. The poet uses it ironically to contrast the mechanical perfection of Swiss clockmaking with the imperfect, chaotic human world these clocks are placed in.

(iv) 'Change of wind' is a metaphor for a sudden, unpredictable shift in political mood, public sentiment, or social atmosphere. Just as a change in wind direction can alter conditions entirely, a change in the prevailing sentiment can disrupt fragile communal peace and reignite dormant tensions.

(v) After a riot, one looks up and sees the clock tower eyeless and silent, its clockwork knocked out, with a zigzag of sky visible through the destroyed structure — an image of devastation and the collapse of the ordered world the clock once represented.

(vi) 'Commemorating' is the apt synonym for 'celebrating' in the extract.

sub_questions.text_english:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:

The trees are in their autumn beauty,
The woodland paths are dry,
Under the October twilight the water
Mirrors a still sky;
Upon the brimming water among the stones
Are nine-and-fifty swans.

The nineteenth autumn has come upon me
Since I first made my count;
I saw, before I had well finished,
All suddenly mount
And scatter wheeling in great broken rings
Upon their clamorous wings.

I have looked upon those brilliant creatures,
And now my heart is sore.
All's changed since I, hearing at twilight,
The first time on this shore,
The bell-beat of their wings above my head,
Trod with a lighter tread,
Unwearied still, lover by lover,
They paddle in the cold
Companionable streams or climb the air;
Their hearts have not grown old;
Passion or conquest, wander where they will,
Attend upon them still.

But now they drift on the still water,
Mysterious, beautiful;
Among what rushes will they build,
By what lake's edge or pool
Delight men's eyes when I awake some day
To find they have flown away ?

(i) What is the theme of this poem ?
(ii) What does the expression 'I first made my count' refer to ?
(iii) What does 'scatter wheeling' refer to ?
(iv) What makes the poet unhappy ?
(v) What is the contrast between the liveliness of the swans and human life ?
(vi) Find the word in the poem which means 'noisy/squawking'.

key_points: (i) The theme is the transience of human life contrasted with the eternal vitality of nature, and the poet's awareness of his own ageing.
(ii) It refers to the first time Yeats counted the swans at Coole Park, nineteen years before the poem's present moment.
(iii) 'Scatter wheeling' refers to the swans suddenly flying up and circling in the sky in broken, scattered formations.
(iv) The poet is unhappy because he has grown old while the swans remain unchanged — still passionate, unwearied and vital.
(v) The swans remain youthful, passionate and full of life, while the poet has aged, become sorrowful and lost his lightness of being.
(vi) 'Clamorous' means noisy/squawking.

sub_questions.solution:
(i) The central theme of Yeats's poem 'The Wild Swans at Coole' is the transience of human life and the relentless passage of time. The poet contrasts his own ageing and growing weariness with the unchanging vitality and beauty of the swans, who appear as timeless as nature itself.

(ii) 'I first made my count' refers to the first time Yeats visited Coole Park and counted the fifty-nine swans on the lake. This was nineteen years before the present moment of the poem, establishing the span of time over which the poet has observed and reflected.

(iii) 'Scatter wheeling' refers to the sudden, dramatic movement of the swans as they all rise into the air at once and wheel across the sky in great broken circles, their wings beating noisily before the poet has finished counting them.

(iv) The poet is made unhappy by the realisation that nineteen years have passed and he has aged significantly, while the swans appear completely unchanged — still unwearied, still passionate, still full of life. His heart is sore with the awareness of his own mortality.

(v) The swans remain eternally youthful — their hearts have not grown old, and passion and conquest still attend them wherever they go. The poet, by contrast, has aged, lost his earlier lightness of tread, and is now filled with sorrow and wistfulness.

(vi) 'Clamorous' is the word in the poem that means noisy or squawking.

sub_questions.text_english: Do you think absolute freedom exists in the world ?

key_points: Define absolute freedom — freedom without any constraints.
Argue that absolute freedom is a philosophical ideal, not a reality.
Every individual operates within social, moral, legal and natural constraints.
Freedom is always relative and defined by its boundaries.
Conclude that meaningful freedom exists within responsible limits.

sub_questions.solution:
Absolute freedom — the complete absence of all constraints — is an appealing ideal but does not exist in practice. Every human being operates within a web of biological, social, legal, and moral limitations. We are free to speak, but not to harm; free to move, but bound by law and geography; free to choose, but constrained by consequence.

Philosophers like Jean-Paul Sartre argued that humans are 'condemned to be free', meaning freedom comes with unavoidable responsibility. True freedom, therefore, is not the absence of limits but the intelligent exercise of choice within them.

Even in the most democratic societies, complete freedom would collapse into chaos. One person's absolute freedom inevitably curtails another's. What does exist, and what is worth cherishing and protecting, is conditional freedom — the liberty to live, think, and act within boundaries that protect the dignity of all. This is the only meaningful form of freedom the world can offer.

sub_questions.text_english: Do you think Prakriti is right in falling in love unilaterally with the monk in order to get rid of the stigma of untouchability ?

key_points: Introduce Prakriti's situation as an untouchable woman seeking dignity.
Acknowledge her love as genuine but the motivation complex.
Discuss whether love driven by a social agenda is truly free love.
Consider the monk's position and the ethics of unilateral love.
Conclude with a balanced view on the justice of her action.

sub_questions.solution:
Prakriti's unilateral love for the Buddhist monk Ananda in Tagore's 'Chandalika' is both understandable and deeply complex. As an untouchable woman, she has lived a life marked by social humiliation and denial of basic human dignity. When Ananda asks her for water without regard for her caste, she experiences — perhaps for the first time — the feeling of being seen as a full human being. Her love, therefore, is not merely romantic but also a desperate reach for recognition and equality.

However, using love as an instrument to escape social stigma raises ethical questions. Love built on an ulterior motive, however justified, can lead to manipulation — as Prakriti's mother's supernatural intervention shows. True freedom from untouchability cannot come through possession of another person.

Prakriti's desire is deeply human and her pain is legitimate, but the means she chooses ultimately reveals that social liberation must come from within, not through another person's love.

sub_questions.text_english: Is R.K. Narayan, the novelist, right in giving his novel the title 'A Tiger for Malgudi' ?

key_points: The title reflects the central character and his journey.
Raja is both a literal tiger and a symbol of power tamed by spirituality.
Malgudi as setting grounds the story in a familiar, human world.
The title captures the novel's central tension between wildness and civilisation.
Narayan's choice is justified as the title encapsulates the novel's theme perfectly.

sub_questions.solution:
R.K. Narayan's choice of title 'A Tiger for Malgudi' is entirely justified and brilliantly apt. The title immediately establishes the novel's central character — Raja, the tiger — and situates him within Malgudi, Narayan's beloved fictional South Indian town that serves as the microcosm of human life.

The title carries multiple layers of meaning. Literally, it refers to Raja's physical presence in Malgudi as a circus tiger and later a free creature. Symbolically, it suggests the idea of a wild, powerful force being introduced into an ordered human community, and the transformation that follows when that force encounters genuine spiritual love.

The tension between Raja's primal nature and the civilised world of Malgudi forms the novel's thematic core. By placing a tiger at the centre of his Malgudi world, Narayan explores themes of spiritual awakening, the relationship between humans and animals, and the redemptive power of compassion. The title is therefore both precise and evocative.

sub_questions.text_english: "Raja's short-lived experience in the children's school and his subsequent rescue brings a complete transformation in Raja's behaviour." Explain.

key_points: Describe Raja's experience in the children's school — chaos and fear he causes.
Explain the rescue by Swamiji and its immediate effect.
Describe the behavioural transformation — from aggression to gentleness.
Connect the transformation to the novel's spiritual theme.
Conclude that the school incident and rescue mark the pivotal turning point in Raja's journey.

sub_questions.solution:
Raja's brief, chaotic entry into the children's school marks a crucial turning point in his journey. When Raja wanders into the school, pandemonium breaks out — children flee in terror, teachers are helpless, and Raja himself is confused and agitated. This incident exposes the fundamental incompatibility between a wild creature and the human world.

It is at this critical moment that Swamiji arrives and transforms the situation entirely. With quiet spiritual authority, he calms Raja without force or fear. Raja, seemingly overwhelmed by the encounter, submits completely to Swamiji's presence. This rescue becomes the catalyst for Raja's spiritual awakening.

Following this, Raja's behaviour changes dramatically. The aggression, the predatory instinct, the restlessness — all gradually fade. He becomes calm, obedient, and almost meditative. The transformation illustrates Narayan's central message that genuine compassion and spiritual power can awaken a higher consciousness even in a wild animal.

sub_questions.text_english: The novel 'The Financial Expert' has two themes — a passion for money and personal love. How are these themes interconnected ?

key_points: Introduce both themes — Margayya's obsession with wealth and his love for his son Balu.
Show how his financial ambition is driven partly by his desire to give Balu a better life.
Demonstrate how the pursuit of money ultimately destroys the personal love he values.
Balu's moral degradation is directly linked to the money-driven world Margayya creates.
Conclude that Narayan shows wealth and love to be incompatible when money becomes an obsession.

sub_questions.solution:
In 'The Financial Expert', R.K. Narayan masterfully intertwines the themes of financial obsession and personal love to show how one inevitably destroys the other. Margayya's relentless pursuit of wealth is partly motivated by his love for his son Balu and his desire to secure a prosperous future for his family. In this sense, the two themes begin as connected — love gives purpose to ambition.

However, as Margayya's obsession with money deepens, it begins to corrode his relationships. He neglects Balu's moral upbringing in his fixation with financial success. Balu, raised in an environment that worships money above all else, grows into a selfish, irresponsible young man whose actions ultimately dismantle everything Margayya has built.

Narayan's irony is devastating: the love that first motivated Margayya's financial ambition is destroyed by that very ambition. The two themes are thus interconnected through their tragic contradiction — wealth pursued in the name of love ultimately consumes it.

sub_questions.text_english: In his novel 'The Financial Expert' the novelist has tried to say that excessive lust for money ends in disaster. Do you agree with this observation ? Support your answer with reference to the events in the novel.

key_points: Agree with the observation and state it clearly.
Describe Margayya's rise through dubious financial dealings.
Show how his obsession leads to moral compromise — the obscene book venture.
Describe the final disasters — Balu's degradation, loss of wealth, family breakdown.
Conclude that the novel is a moral parable about the destructiveness of unrestrained greed.

sub_questions.solution:
I fully agree with the observation that Narayan's 'The Financial Expert' is a moral parable about the disastrous consequences of excessive greed. Margayya begins as a small-time financial advisor under a banyan tree, driven by an almost pathological desire for wealth and social status.

His single-minded obsession leads him to make increasingly compromised choices. He partners with the unscrupulous Dr. Pal to publish an obscene book, prioritising financial gain over ethical considerations. Though this makes him wealthy, it plants the seeds of disaster — Balu, his beloved son, is corrupted by the same moral vacuum that surrounds their money-driven household.

Balu's reckless behaviour, his failed marriage, and his hostility towards his father ultimately strip Margayya of everything he had accumulated. The novel ends with Margayya returning to his original spot under the banyan tree, having lost his wealth, his dignity, and his family's happiness. Narayan's message is clear and unambiguous: money pursued as an end in itself inevitably destroys the very things that give life meaning.
